implementation_notes: Noda Time provides the range object itself: DateInterval is constructed from two LocalDate values (or a start and a duration), is explicitly closed - the end date is part of the interval - and exposes Contains(LocalDate), Contains(DateInterval), Intersection, Union and Length, so Effectivity becomes an object holding one DateInterval plus the as-of predicate. LocalDate is a calendar date without time or zone and converts to System.DateOnly on .NET 8+. Choose it whenever a real calendar model is wanted (different calendar systems, offsets, durations); the .NET 6 DateOnly route replaces the library when the project may not take the dependency.
pitfalls: DateInterval is closed while calendar APIs and PostgreSQL ranges are half-open: mixing the two conventions in one codebase double-counts the changeover date.
DateInterval equality is component-wise and no ordering is defined for it, so sorting periods means ordering by Start explicitly.
LocalDate carries a calendar system; DateInterval throws when start and end use different calendars, which happens easily when one bound comes from a DateTime with a non-Gregorian calendar.

variants.name: .NET 6 DateOnly record struct
variants.implementation_notes: With .NET 6 DateOnly removes the time component from DateTime and cannot be shifted by a time zone, which is the correct representation for date-granularity validity; the range itself is then a small readonly record struct with From and a nullable Until (null meaning "until further notice") plus two methods. Choose this variant when no calendar library may be added; the classic DateInterval-style structure stays justified when calendar systems, offsets or span arithmetic matter, because DateOnly is always proleptic Gregorian and carries no zone.
variants.idiom_name: System.DateOnly bounds in a readonly record struct with contains()/overlaps()
pitfalls: Until is nullable, so every predicate must handle null; a single forgotten check makes the common open-ended period match nothing.
default(DateOnly) is 0001-01-01: an uninitialised field looks like a plausible start date instead of missing data.
Converting a DateOnly to a DateTime (ToDateTime(TimeOnly.MinValue)) reintroduces a time and a Kind, and storing that value in a datetime column can shift the day across zones or DST.
